title: PHP in Late 2026: Why 8.5.12 Matters and What 8.6 Changes Next
author: Mister Jack
summary: PHP updates are easy to ignore when an application is already working. That is especially true when a release looks like another small version number: 8.5.11 → 8.5.12 But PHP 8.5.12 is not the kind of update I would treat as routine maintenance. It is a security release addressing two critical vulnerabilities that PHP says can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. At the same time, PHP 8.6 is moving through its release-candidate cycle, giving developers an early look at where the language is heading next. From a tech-review perspective, these two developments are interesting for different reasons. PHP 8.5.12 matters because of security now. PHP 8.6 matters because of what developers should prepare for next. PHP 8.5.12 is primarily a security update PHP 8.5.12 was announced in October 2026 as a security release. The PHP team says it fixes two critical vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619 Both can potentially allow unauthenticated remote code execution. More importantly, the PHP team explicitly recommends that PHP 8.5 users update immediately and says there are no complete mitigations that replace upgrading. Source: PHP.net That changes how I would classify this release. This is not: “Upgrade when you have time.” It is closer to: “Test the patch quickly and move production systems to the fixed version.” For applications exposed to the public internet, remote-code-execution vulnerabilities are among the issues I would take most seriously. Small version number, big security implications One of the biggest mistakes teams can make with runtime updates is judging importance by version number. A patch release can look insignificant. But patch releases often contain exactly the type of security and stability work production systems need. The PHP 8.5.12 changelog includes fixes across the core runtime and other components, including memory-safety, crashes, garbage collection, CLI behavior, and other runtime issues. Source: PHP 8 Changelog Most developers will never interact directly with many of those bugs. That does not make them irrelevant. Infrastructure software often works best when developers barely notice it. The problem is that vulnerabilities can remain invisible until someone actively exploits them. Who should care about PHP 8.5.12? The obvious answer is anyone already running PHP 8.5. But I would think about this at several levels. Public web applications If a PHP application accepts requests from the public internet, security patches should be treated as operational work rather than optional framework maintenance. SaaS platforms A vulnerability in the runtime affects the foundation below the application. Even a well-designed Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, or custom PHP application still depends on the PHP runtime underneath it. Agencies managing client sites Agencies often maintain dozens or hundreds of environments. The important question is not simply: “Do we support PHP 8.5?” It becomes: “Which environments are on vulnerable builds, and how quickly can we patch them safely?” Self-hosted applications Teams operating their own servers should verify the actual PHP runtime version in production rather than assuming package managers or hosting panels have already updated it. Updating still requires testing Urgent security update does not mean: “Push directly to production without checking anything.” A disciplined upgrade process still matters. I would normally want to see: the PHP runtime updated in staging automated tests executed critical user flows tested logs checked for new warnings or errors framework and extension compatibility reviewed production deployed quickly after validation Security urgency should shorten the upgrade window. It should not eliminate engineering discipline. The broader point: runtime security is part of application security Developers often think about security at the application level: authentication authorization SQL injection XSS API permissions input validation Those are important. But application security also depends on: programming language runtime operating system web server database third-party packages container images extensions If any layer contains a critical vulnerability, secure application code alone may not be enough. This is why dependency and runtime maintenance should be considered part of normal software engineering. Not just infrastructure housekeeping. Then there is PHP 8.6 While PHP 8.5.12 is about production security, PHP 8.6 is about what comes next. As of late October 2026, PHP 8.6.0 RC4 is available for testing. The PHP team explicitly says RC4 is an early test version and should not be used in production. The next and final release candidate, RC5, is currently planned for November 5, 2026. Source: PHP 2026 Release Archive That distinction is important. A release candidate is useful for: testing applications finding compatibility issues validating frameworks checking extensions preparing libraries reporting bugs It is not the version I would deploy to a production SaaS application just because I want the latest PHP. Why developers should test PHP 8.6 before stable release Waiting until the stable release before testing can create unnecessary pressure. If you maintain a large PHP application, trying the release candidate in CI or a test environment can reveal: deprecated behavior extension incompatibilities dependency problems framework issues warnings changed runtime behavior That gives teams time to fix problems before the production upgrade becomes urgent. For library and framework maintainers, pre-release testing matters even more. Their compatibility work affects thousands of downstream applications. PHP has changed significantly over the last few releases One reason I find current PHP interesting is that the language has been gradually moving away from the old stereotype of being a loosely structured scripting language. PHP 8.5, released in 2025, introduced several notable features. These include: a new URI extension the pipe operator clone-with syntax #[NoDiscard] broader support for closures and first-class callables in constant expressions Source: PHP 8.5 Release Notes The pipe operator is probably the most visually obvious example. Instead of deeply nested function calls, developers can express a sequence of transformations from left to right. That does not fundamentally change what PHP can build. But it can improve how certain transformations are expressed and read. Modern PHP is less about syntax and more about ecosystem maturity When people debate whether PHP is still relevant, the conversation often becomes too focused on language syntax. I think that misses the bigger picture. The more useful questions are: Is the runtime actively maintained? Are security releases shipped quickly? Do frameworks have healthy ecosystems? Can teams build maintainable applications? Are modern deployment workflows supported? Can the language scale with the organization using it? PHP remains deeply connected to a massive amount of web infrastructure. That includes traditional CMS platforms, custom applications, SaaS platforms, ecommerce systems, and modern framework-based products. The interesting part is not whether PHP feels fashionable. It is whether the stack remains operationally and technically useful. What I would do if I managed a PHP application today If I were already on PHP 8.5 I would prioritize moving to PHP 8.5.12 because of the security fixes. If I were on an older supported PHP branch I would check the security release available for that branch rather than assuming PHP 8.5.12 is the correct direct upgrade target. If I were preparing for PHP 8.6 I would start testing RC4 in non-production environments. Not because RC4 should be deployed. But because finding compatibility issues before stable release is usually easier than discovering them during a production migration. Framework teams should test early For Laravel, Symfony, WordPress plugin developers, package maintainers, and other PHP ecosystem developers, a new major release has broader consequences. It is not just: “Does my application boot?” I would also test: CLI commands queues scheduled jobs database drivers caching mail authentication file processing image libraries third-party extensions test suites A framework may technically support a PHP version while one specific extension or package still creates problems. That is why production-readiness is an ecosystem question, not just a runtime question. Do not confuse “new” with “production ready” This is probably the most important distinction around PHP 8.6 right now. Developers naturally want to try the newest version. That is useful. But the correct place for RC4 is: development CI testing compatibility validation Not critical production infrastructure. PHP itself explicitly warns against using the current release candidate in production. That is advice I would follow. My view as a tech reviewer What stands out to me about PHP in late 2026 is not one flashy feature. It is the contrast between two different parts of the release lifecycle. PHP 8.5.12 This is about production responsibility . If your environment is affected, security should take priority over feature discussions. PHP 8.6 RC4 This is about preparation . Developers should test it, frameworks should validate compatibility, and maintainers should identify problems before the stable release. Those are two very different reasons to care about a PHP release. And treating them differently is part of good engineering practice. Is PHP still moving forward? I think so. PHP 8.5 already added features such as the URI extension, pipe operator, clone-with syntax, and #[NoDiscard] , while the PHP 8.6 cycle shows that the language continues to evolve through regular release testing and maintenance. But I would not judge the health of PHP based only on new syntax. The stronger signal is that the ecosystem continues to receive: security patches runtime fixes language improvements release candidates compatibility testing A mature technology does not need to reinvent itself every year. It needs to keep becoming safer, easier to maintain, and more predictable to operate. Final thoughts If you use PHP today, there are really two conversations happening. PHP 8.5.12: Update because security matters. PHP 8.6 RC4: Test it because the next generation of the runtime is getting closer, but do not use the release candidate in production. For me, the bigger lesson is simple: Runtime maintenance is part of software engineering. Framework choice, architecture, clean code, and testing matter. But if the runtime underneath the application has a critical security issue, keeping it patched becomes one of the most important technical decisions the team can make.

title: The Unreasonable Length of HTML
author: Andrew Chemis
summary: Originally published on andrewchemis.dev . In May, Thariq Shihipar argued on the Claude Code blog that agents should hand people HTML instead of Markdown ( The unreasonable effectiveness of HTML ). He finds it "difficult to read a Markdown file of more than a hundred lines", and HTML carries the charts, diagrams and layouts Markdown can't. Then the line that sold me: "the chance of someone actually reading your spec, report, or PR writeup is much higher if it's in HTML." I agree with nearly all of it. Lede , which stands for Line-Encoded Document Engine, is what I built after reading it. What it cuts is the HTML itself; the model never writes any. His FAQ takes the obvious question head on ("Isn't it less efficient?") and grants that Markdown "often uses fewer tokens". Then it adds that "with the 1MM context window in Opus 4.7, the increased token usage is not really noticeable in the context window." About the window, he's right. Ten HTML pages come to about 51,000 tokens, which is 5% of a million. The tokens cost something everywhere else, though, and once I measured it I couldn't stop seeing it. What the extra tokens cost I had Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 each write 60 pages twice from the same briefs, once as HTML and once as Lede, and counted output tokens with each model's own tokenizer. Mean output per page was 2,770 against 598 for Haiku, 4,501 against 625 for Sonnet, and 5,068 against 713 for Opus. Turned into what a reader of this blog would pay for: Cost: 1,000 pages from Opus 5.5 come to $101 of output tokens as HTML and $14 as Lede, at list price. On Sonnet 5.5 it's $45 against $6. That counts the page's own tokens only, not thinking or the reference the model reads first. Time: output arrives one token at a time. At an assumed 60 tokens a second, Opus takes about 84 seconds to finish an HTML page and about 12 to finish the Lede one. Context: the 51,000 tokens above against about 7,000, which is small in a million tokens but still gets re-read on every later turn of the session. Review: one benchmark page is 136 lines of HTML and 32 lines of Lede. The last one matters to me more than the bill. The HTML source of a page is mostly class names and style rules, so it runs well past the hundred lines he stops reading at, and it's the part I'd want to check before the page goes anywhere. A Lede file is content from the first line to the last, close enough to Markdown that a diff of it reads like a diff of a document. The rendered page is the same kind of page his post argues for. This is a whole one: @title Checkout, week 42 @subtitle p99 latency is back under its target after Tuesday's cache fix kpi p99 latency | 182 ms | -38% | good kpi Error rate | 0.12% | -0.4 pts | good kpi Deploys | 23 | +4 | neutral data lat = day,p99; Mon,240; Tue,296; Wed,190; Thu,184; Fri,182 chart line lat unit=ms target="200 SLO" mark="Tue cache fix" title="p99 latency by day" ! The cache now expires on write instead of on a timer, so a deploy no longer serves stale prices. That's 214 tokens. The compiler turns it into a 44 KB page with a title block, three metric tiles, a line chart with a dashed target and an event marker, a note, light and dark themes, a phone layout, and no script tag. There's a second reason I wanted the model out of the HTML. An agent that has read an email or a web page can be talked into writing a <script> tag or an image URL that leaks data, and a page is the obvious place for it. Lede has no way to say either. The compiler sanitizes its one escape hatch for raw HTML, refuses remote images unless asked, and writes a content security policy into every page. Five kinds of page, twelve examples The examples on the site come straight from his post. It sorts HTML artifacts into five kinds (specs and planning, code review, design and prototypes, reports and explainers, custom editing interfaces), and I gave Sonnet 5.5 twelve of his example prompts with nothing but the Lede reference. Each of the twelve examples on the site shows the request, the page and its full source, and says what the page couldn't do. An early release Lede is an early release, and it isn't as refined or hardened as it could be. It fails in a few areas, and where it loses on looks the site says so. On the benchmark task behind the 32-line figure, both blind judges preferred the HTML, for its projected trend line and grouped cards. Against each model's own HTML, Lede pages won or tied 60% of the time for Haiku, 22% for Opus and 10% for Sonnet. That table is on the front page under the heading "Cheaper and safer. Not yet as good as the best HTML." That is where it stands today, and there is a lot of room to improve and refine it. Using it I've been using Lede on my own projects, and it has earned its place as a way to put something in front of a person for approval: the page they read before they say yes. I'm also convinced it reduces token usage, and the benchmark above is the part of that I've measured. I'm excited to see how people use the format and to learn from it, including the uses I didn't plan for. The code is open source at github.com/lede-lang/lede . It installs two ways. From npm, @lede-lang/cli gives you the lede command. As a skill, the Claude plugin marketplace in the repository takes /plugin marketplace add lede-lang/lede and then /plugin install lede@lede . Try it The site is at ledelang.dev , the code is at github.com/lede-lang/lede , and the playground is the quickest way to try Lede. You type Lede on the left and the page appears on the right, so you can load one of the examples and change a line. If you have a page Lede can't draw, tell me. Each example lists what its page couldn't do, and that list is the roadmap.

title: A Stranger Writes Half of My AI Matcher's Prompt
author: Nabeel Hassan
summary: Every night a cron job in Upwork Scout, my job-alert side project, asks Claude Haiku how well a freelance job fits a specific freelancer. The prompt has two halves. One half is the freelancer's own profile. The other half is the job post: title, budget, skills, client stats and up to 1,400 characters of description. I did not write that description. A stranger on Upwork did. It lands in the model's context next to my scoring rules, and the model has no reliable way to tell my instructions apart from text that merely sits near them. That is the whole AI security problem in one paragraph. We tend to argue about prompt wording; the fixes that work are boring engineering around the model, the same rules you apply to any input you did not write. Code and data stopped being separate Normal software keeps a clear line. Code decides what happens; data gets processed. A language model erases that line. Your instructions, the user's question, a retrieved document and an uploaded file all arrive as one stream of text, and the model acts on all of it. Two things follow. Anyone who can put text in front of the model has some influence over what it does. And the output is generated, not looked up, so you cannot fully predict it. The direct version of prompt injection is a user typing "ignore your instructions". The one that matters more is indirect: the instruction rides inside content the model reads on someone's behalf, like an email, a knowledge base document, a support ticket or a job post. No prompt wording reliably fixes this. So I stopped asking "can it be injected?" and started asking a better question. What is the worst an injected instruction can do? Design so the answer is small. For the Upwork Scout matcher, it is honestly small: The model can read one job and one profile, and that profile belongs to the user being scored. There is no tool, no database access, no other account in the context. Its output is forced into a fixed shape with structured outputs: an integer score and a string reason , with additionalProperties: false . My code then clamps the score to 0 to 100, cuts the reason to 200 characters, and returns null on any failure so that job falls back to plain filter matching. const parsed = JSON . parse ( text ) as { score : number ; reason : string }; const score = Math . max ( 0 , Math . min ( 100 , Math . round ( Number ( parsed . score )))); if ( ! Number . isFinite ( score )) return null ; return { score , reason : String ( parsed . reason || "" ). slice ( 0 , 200 ) }; So the worst case is a job post that talks its way to a 100 with a glowing one-line reason, landing at the top of somebody's alert email. That is a real failure. A freelancer could spend Connects on a bad job because my ranking told them to. But it is a bounded failure. Nobody's data leaves, nothing gets written, and the damage is one row in one email. Compare that with a feature that can query the whole account, or one with write tools. Same injection, very different worst case. That is why the first control is not in the prompt at all: limit what the feature can reach, and keep authority in your application, decided by the signed-in user's permissions rather than by whatever the model concludes from the conversation. I wrote about the write-tools case separately in giving an AI agent write access one verb at a time , and about a voice-agent version of the read case in the lookup tool that just took a phone number . The model's output is user input This is the rule I wish more teams internalized. Whatever the model returns should be handled like input from an unknown user, because partly it is. A stranger's text shaped it. In Upwork Scout, that reason string goes two places: the alert email and the dashboard. The dashboard is React, so the string is rendered as text by default. The email is a hand-built HTML template, so the reason goes through the same tiny escape function as the job title and description: function esc ( s : string ): string { return s . replace ( /&/g , " & " ). replace ( /</g , " < " ). replace ( />/g , " > " ); } Nothing clever. The point is that model output takes the same path as every other untrusted string, not a special "it came from our AI, it is fine" path. The rendering risk is worse when your UI renders rich text. A model can be steered into producing a markdown image or link whose URL carries user data in the query string. The moment the page loads that image, the data has left your system without anyone clicking anything. If you render model output as markdown, restrict link destinations, do not auto-load external images, and escape HTML by default. The same applies downstream. If output feeds a query, a spreadsheet, an email or code that runs, validate it at that boundary. Data leaks are usually correct answers The most damaging failure in a business AI feature is rarely a weird answer. It is a correct answer built from data the user should never have seen. Three places this happens: Retrieval without permissions. If your search step pulls from everything and relies on the model to hold back what the user cannot see, it eventually will not. Filter at fetch time so restricted passages never reach the context. More on that in your RAG demo works because someone picked the documents . Shared context across tenants. Shared caches, shared conversation memory and batch jobs that group requests across customers are the classic spots where one account's data shows up in another's answer. Every call should be assembled from one tenant's data only. Training on user content. A model cannot keep a secret it was trained on. That is one more reason I keep business facts in retrieval or the prompt, not in weights, as I argued in fine-tuning your facts is hardcoding them into a binary . Your endpoint is an open tab A public AI feature is a model someone else pays for. People will try to use your support bot as a free general assistant, push huge inputs through it, or script it. Here Upwork Scout is a mixed report card, and I would rather be honest about it. The nightly matcher only runs on jobs that already passed the user's hard filters, verdicts are cached per user and job, and there is a cap of 150 AI scores per user per day. That part is in good shape, and the cost side is in cheap filters first, LLM last . The profile import endpoint, where a user pastes their Upwork profile and Claude structures it into fields, requires a signed-in session and truncates input to 24,000 characters, but it has no per-user rate limit yet. Writing this post is how I noticed. It is on the list. Basic controls cover most of this: per-user and per-account rate limits, input size limits, sign-in for expensive actions, a narrow scope that declines unrelated requests, and spending alerts on the provider account. The broader cost story is in model calls are metered . Logs are the leak nobody plans for For every vendor you send data to, know what you send, whether they retain it, whether it trains anything, and where it is processed. Then look at your own logs. Prompts and responses are gold for debugging, so keep them, but they contain whatever users typed and whatever your system retrieved. They need the same access control, retention and redaction as the database the data came from. A side note from my own matcher: on failure it logs only the job ID and the error message, not the prompt, which is the kind of decision that is easy to make on day one and annoying to retrofit. A test pass you can actually run Before launch, and again whenever the model, the prompt or a data source changes: Injection attempts through every input path: direct messages, uploads, retrieved documents and any third-party content the feature reads. For me, that means a job post written to game the score. Cross-account checks: sign in as customer A and try to surface customer B's data through the AI feature. Prompt extraction: get the system prompt out, then confirm nothing in it hurts. Rendering tests: links, images and markup the model was steered into producing. Abuse tests: hit the rate limits and confirm the spending alerts fire. A log review: what is stored, who can read it, when it is deleted. The takeaway AI features are not secured by clever prompts. They are secured the way the rest of your app is: access decided in your own code, untrusted input and output treated as untrusted, each component limited in what it can reach, and a clear picture of where data goes. Do that from version one and the model's unpredictability becomes a quality problem instead of an incident. The longer, less code-heavy version of this, written for founders evaluating a team building AI into their product, is on the Null Studio blog: AI feature security . What is the worst thing an injected instruction could do in a feature you have shipped? I am curious how many of us have actually written that answer down.

title: How GPUI's Entity Model Solves Rust State Management (With a Ratatui Example)
author: Mouhamad Al Mounayar
summary: Introduction Gpui has been gaining a lot of popularity these last couple of months, and I am proud to say I have been a fan of the framework long before that. As a matter of fact, here is a tweet by me saying that people should talk about it more (when people didn't talk about it more): In my opinion, two things are contributing to the popularity of the framework today: Performance: I think it is clear to everyone now that gpui is the best alternative to electron applications. AI: Many people hate using Rust because of the borrow checker, but with agents, they no longer have to deal with it as much. What I really loved about the framework, however, is its approach to state management. When I first started building terminal user interfaces with Rust, I struggled with how I should approach state management, because with Rust (unlike JavaScript) the borrow checker makes things especially hard. After seeing how gpui handled this, by studying the codebase and reading this gem of an article , I noticed that the approach adopted can be transferred to any other application which wants to manage state effectively. In this blog post, I will share how I built an experimental state management crate for Rust, and I will use it to build an application with ratatui. State Management Crate Our state management crate creates a state. It provides components of the application with ways to read and update said state. In Rust, each variable has a unique owner. So, in order to avoid the complexity that comes with the borrow checker, the state is going to be owned by one App object. Instead of multiple components holding references to the state owned by the App , the App gives out cheap handles to the components which want to read or update it. This is possible because the App stores its entities in a SlotMap data structure. A SlotMap is an array which allows O(1) insertion and retrieval of elements by key. A key is returned after inserting a value, and the key will always refer to the value which was inserted. This makes it ideal for storing our application entities. For our use case, the slotmap crate is used. With that dependency in place, we can start building our crate, beginning with the App struct that owns everything. App So, let us define the App struct as follows: pub struct App { map : SlotMap < DefaultKey , Option < Box < dyn Any >>> } DefaultKey is the type of the key returned after inserting values into the SlotMap . Values are Option<Box<dyn Any>> , since a state can be anything; wrapping it in an Option is useful for preventing reentrant updates. Entity Next, let's define what an Entity is. In gpui, Entity represents the handle that the App gives out. It basically contains the key of the value inserted into the slotmap , a ref_count to count how many times the entity was cloned, and a PhantomData which specifies which type the Entity holds. pub struct Entity < T > { entity_id : DefaultKey , ref_count : Rc < () > , _marker : PhantomData < T > } With this, we can implement a method to register new entities. impl App { fn new < T : 'static > ( & mut self , build : impl FnOnce ( & App ) -> T ) -> Entity < T > { let state = build ( self ); let entity_id = self .map .insert ( Some ( Box :: new ( state ))); Entity { entity_id , ref_count : Rc :: new (()), _marker : PhantomData } } } As you can see, the method accepts a closure which is handed a reference to the App . This is because some entities might need to be initialised with data from other entities in App . Let us now implement a method to read from a state. impl App { pub fn read < T : 'static > ( & self , entity : & Entity < T > ) -> & T { let value = self .map .get ( entity .entity_id ) .expect ( "stale handle" ); match value { Some ( value ) => value .downcast_ref :: < T > () .unwrap (), None => { panic! ( "cannot read a value which is currently being updated" ) } } } } SlotMap::get returns None when the key isn't present in the map. This happens if the entity was removed (and the slot's generation bumped), or if the handle is simply invalid. We expect here rather than propagate the error, because reaching this state should never happen in a correctly-behaving program. If it does, it signals a bug in our architecture, not a recoverable condition. Since this is an experimental crate, we're choosing to fail loudly rather than handle every edge case gracefully. The next step is to implement an update method in order to update entities. impl App { pub fn update < T : 'static , R > ( & mut self , entity : Entity < T > , update : impl FnOnce ( & mut T , & mut App ) -> R , ) -> R { let value = self .map .get_mut ( entity .entity_id ) .expect ( "stale handle" ); let boxed = value .take () .expect ( "entity already being updated" ); let mut state : T = * boxed .downcast :: < T > () .unwrap (); let result : R = update ( & mut state , self ); * self .map .get_mut ( entity .entity_id ) .unwrap () = Some ( Box :: new ( state )); result } } The method receives a closure which is yielded a mutable reference to the entity it wants to update. The expect after take panics in case of reentrancy: if the entity is already being updated, we cannot call update on it again. This is why we chose to use Option as the value type in the SlotMap . It gives us a way to signal that this value is not available right now. Dropping stale entities When there are no more handles pointing to a state in the map, the state is marked as stale and should be removed. To achieve this, we add a pending field to our App struct to keep track of the stale entities: pub struct App { map : SlotMap < DefaultKey , Option < Box < dyn Any >>> , pending : Rc < RefCell < Vec < DefaultKey >>> } When an entity handle is dropped, it checks if it is the only handle remaining to the state. If no other handle remains, it pushes its entity_id onto the pending queue. Entity should have access to the pending queue. We give it a Weak reference rather than an Rc , so that holding an Entity never keeps App 's queue (and thus App itself) artificially alive: pub struct Entity < T > { entity_id : DefaultKey , ref_count : Rc < () > , pending : Weak < RefCell < Vec < DefaultKey >>> , _marker : PhantomData < T > } With this new field in place, we need to update new_entity to populate it whenever an entity is created: pub fn new_entity < T : 'static > ( & mut self , build : impl FnOnce ( & App ) -> T ) -> Entity < T > { let entity = build ( self ); let entity_id = self .map .insert ( Some ( Box :: new ( entity ))); Entity { entity_id , ref_count : Rc :: new (()), pending : Rc :: downgrade ( & self .pending ), _marker : PhantomData , } } Then we implement Drop for Entity , so that when the last handle to a state goes out of scope, its slot is queued for removal: impl < T > Drop for Entity < T > { fn drop ( & mut self ) { if Rc :: strong_count ( & self .ref_count ) == 1 && let Some ( queue ) = self .pending .upgrade () { queue .borrow_mut () .push ( self .entity_id ); } } } Finally, we implement a method called flush_entities which drains the queue and actually removes those stale slots from the map: impl App { pub fn flush_entities ( & mut self ) { let ids : Vec < DefaultKey > = self .pending .borrow_mut () .drain ( .. ) .collect (); for id in ids { self .map .remove ( id ); } } } Usage Let's test our framework by creating a simple Ratatui application. In the majority of applications, one component updates a state, and another one reads from that state. In our test application, we will demonstrate this by creating two widgets. One will act as an input and update an input_buffer . The second widget will just read the input_buffer and reflect its changes (In real world applications, this second widget might use the input to filter search results for example). We will start by creating a Root struct. The Root struct holds a reference to an App struct: struct Root < 'a > { app : & 'a mut App , widgets : Vec < Box < dyn Component >> } The Root also holds a list of widgets, defined using the Component trait. We define the Component trait as follows: trait Component { fn render_with_cx ( & mut self , cx : & mut App , frame : & mut Frame , area : Rect ); fn handle_key ( & mut self , cx : & mut App , key : KeyEvent ); } Each component uses render_with_cx to draw on the frame while still having access to the context. Components also define a handle_key method in order to handle events. Let us create our two widgets with their implementations of Component . struct InputWidget { input_buffer : Entity < String > , } struct EchoWidget { input_buffer : Entity < String > , } Each widget owns an Entity<String> . The input widget updates input_buffer and the echo widget reads it and displays it. impl InputWidget { fn init ( input_buffer : Entity < String > ) -> Self { Self { input_buffer } } } impl EchoWidget { fn init ( input_buffer : Entity < String > ) -> Self { Self { input_buffer } } } impl Component for InputWidget { fn render_with_cx ( & mut self , cx : & mut App , frame : & mut Frame , area : Rect ) { let block = Block :: bordered () .title ( "Input" ) .padding ( Padding :: uniform ( 1 )); let inner = block .inner ( area ); block .render ( area , frame .buffer_mut ()); let input_buffer = cx .read ( & self .input_buffer ); let text_width = input_buffer .chars () .count () as u16 ; frame .set_cursor_position ( Position :: new ( inner .x + text_width , inner .y )); Paragraph :: new ( & input_buffer [ .. ]) .wrap ( Wrap { trim : false }) .render ( inner , frame .buffer_mut ()); } fn handle_key ( & mut self , cx : & mut App , key : KeyEvent ) { match key .code { KeyCode :: Char ( c ) => cx .update ( self .input_buffer .clone (), | input_buffer , _cx | { input_buffer .push ( c ); }), KeyCode :: Backspace => cx .update ( self .input_buffer .clone (), | input_buffer , _cx | { if input_buffer .len () > 0 { input_buffer .remove ( input_buffer .len () - 1 ); } }), _ => {} } } } In render_with_cx we render a block and a paragraph. To learn more about widgets and how to render them, you can check the ratatui documentation. The interesting part is that the paragraph is initialised with the input_buffer contents, thus the call to cx.read(&self.input_buffer) . In handle_key we listen to key events and then update our input_buffer state with cx.update() . The EchoWidget component only reads the input buffer entity and displays it: impl Component for EchoWidget { fn render_with_cx ( & mut self , cx : & mut App , frame : & mut Frame , area : Rect ) { let block = Block :: bordered () .title ( "Echo" ) .padding ( Padding :: uniform ( 1 )); let inner = block .inner ( area ); block .render ( area , frame .buffer_mut ()); let input_buffer = cx .read ( & self .input_buffer ); Paragraph :: new ( & input_buffer [ .. ]) .wrap ( Wrap { trim : false }) .render ( inner , frame .buffer_mut ()); } // Echo widget is read-only: it never receives input focus or key events. fn handle_key ( & mut self , _cx : & mut App , _key : KeyEvent ) {} } Entity creation happens when initialising the Root struct by calling cx.new_entity : impl < 'a > Root < 'a > { fn init ( cx : & 'a mut App ) -> Root < 'a > { let input_buffer = cx .new_entity (| _ | "Enter Text" .into ()); Root { app : cx , widgets : vec! [ Box :: new ( InputWidget :: init ( input_buffer .clone ())), Box :: new ( EchoWidget :: init ( input_buffer .clone ())), ], } } } We also define a run method for Root which does the drawing by calling the render_with_cx method on each component, and listens for events by calling handle_key_event on each component in the root. impl < 'a > Root < 'a > { fn run ( & mut self , terminal : & mut DefaultTerminal ) -> anyhow :: Result < () > { loop { self .app .flush_entities (); let _ = terminal .draw (| frame | { let [ top , bottom ] = Layout :: vertical ([ Constraint :: Percentage ( 50 ), Constraint :: Percentage ( 50 )]) .areas ( frame .area ()); self .widgets [ 0 ] .render_with_cx ( self .app , frame , top ); self .widgets [ 1 ] .render_with_cx ( self .app , frame , bottom ); }); if let Event :: Key ( key_event ) = event :: read () ? { if ! key_event .is_press () { continue ; } let is_quit = key_event .code == KeyCode :: Esc || ( key_event .code == KeyCode :: Char ( 'c' ) && key_event .modifiers .contains ( KeyModifiers :: CONTROL )); if is_quit { break Ok (()); } // Only the input widget (top, index 0) is interactive. self .widgets [ 0 ] .handle_key ( self .app , key_event ); } } } } Finally, we define our main function: fn main () { let mut app : App = App :: init (); let mut root = Root :: init ( & mut app ); let _ = ratatui :: run (| terminal | root .run ( terminal )); } Conclusion Using our state management crate inspired by gpui, we were able to effectively manage state without dealing with the complexities that the borrow checker brings. Rather than wrapping each piece of shared state in an Rc<RefCell<T>> , as is common in Rust UI code, our state lives in a single SlotMap owned by the App . Components simply hold cheap Entity<T> handles into that map, instead of sharing mutable references directly. The state management crate we developed here is experimental. It could be enhanced with other features, mainly: Only redraw when the UI is marked as dirty, instead of each frame. Components subscribing to/observing a certain state. (We didn't have to deal with this here, since we redraw the entire UI each tick.) Code is available on GitHub: State Management Crate Test Application

title: 70% of Philippine AI Adopters Are Still on Basic Use
author: Yano.AI Technologies Inc.
summary: More than 396,000 businesses in the Philippines now use AI, 32 percent of firms, up from 21 percent a year earlier (Source: Strand Partners for AWS, 2026). Seventy percent of those adopters are still limited to public chatbots, routine productivity apps, and off-the-shelf AI products (Source: Strand Partners for AWS, 2026). The adoption number is real. The depth is not. The Adoption Number Is Real The AWS-commissioned study surveyed 1,000 Philippine business leaders and 1,000 members of the public (Source: Strand Partners for AWS, 2026). A Philippine Institute for Development Studies study found only 14.9 percent of firms use AI tools, concentrated among large urban firms in ICT and BPO (Source: PIDS, 2024). The figures use different samples and definitions. The hardware is already in place. 90.8 percent of establishments own computers and 81 percent have internet access (Source: PIDS, 2024). MSMEs were 99.63 percent of registered establishments in 2023 and 66.97 percent of employment (Source: DTI, 2024). Hardware is not the bottleneck. The Depth Problem Among businesses already using AI, adoption splits three ways: 70 percent sit at basic use, 18 percent have integrated AI across multiple functions, and 12 percent run custom AI systems, agentic AI, or autonomous technology (Source: Strand Partners for AWS, 2026). Among those adopters, 74 percent report productivity gains and 68 percent say revenue rose, with average revenue growth of 20 percent (Source: AWS press release, 2026). Yet 57 percent are still experimenting, only 17 percent have a formal scaling roadmap, and just 12 percent have a comprehensive AI governance framework (Source: AWS press release, 2026). Digital skills shortages topped the barrier list at 47 percent (Source: AWS press release, 2026). Compare a scaled deployment. Store Genie, built by PLDT Home and Smart Communications with Amdocs, supports more than 750 frontline agents across 149 locations and cut some order workflows from hours to minutes (Source: AWS via AI4Philippines, 2026). That is the shape of the 12 percent. What the First AI Bill Looks Like Most Philippine SMEs will start with a subscription. Google Workspace Business Starter runs $7.00 per user per month on a one-year commitment, Business Standard is $14.00 per user per month, and Business Plus is $22.00 per user per month, billed in US dollars with tax excluded (Source: Google, 2026). A five-person microenterprise on Starter spends $35 a month, or $420 a year, roughly PHP 26,700 at the Bangko Sentral reference rate of PHP 63.60 to the dollar (Source: BSP, 2026). The DTI classifies micro enterprises as those holding up to PHP 3 million in assets with one to nine employees (Source: DTI, 2024), so this is the typical budget for the country's smallest businesses. Spending money is easy. Deciding which workflow to hand to a tool, and how to tell whether it worked, is the part that needs a plan. Local Models and the Zero-Subscription Route Some AI tools now run on hardware you already own. Survival LLM is an open-source assistant and reference library that runs on your own computer and keeps working with the internet off, so questions never leave the machine (Source: Survival LLM, 2026). Its library carries roughly 1.5 million articles from Wikipedia, WikiMed, MedlinePlus, CDC, FEMA, and WHO (Source: Survival LLM, 2026). Model choice follows available memory. 16 to 31 GB of RAM gets an IBM Granite 4.2 8B model on a 6 GB download, while 128 GB gets Nemotron 3.5 Super on 80 GB (Source: Survival LLM, 2026). In the project's blind evaluation against USDA, CDC, FEMA, EPA, NHS and WHO guidance, Nemotron Super scored 86 percent accuracy with zero harmful answers, Qwen3.8 27B scored 80 percent, and Granite 4.2 8B scored 55 percent (Source: Survival LLM, 2026). The business case is narrow. Subscription cost falls to zero and customer data never leaves the building, but the cost moves to hardware and attention: a 16 GB machine gives you a 55 percent accurate model on a narrow question set, not a general assistant. The Part Nobody Plans: Personal Data The National Privacy Commission issued Advisory No. 2024-04 on December 19, 2024, setting out how the Data Privacy Act of 2012 applies to AI systems that process personal data (Source: NPC, 2024). NPC Circular No. 2022-04 covers registration of data processing systems, notification of automated decision-making or profiling, and designation of a data protection officer (Source: NPC, 2022). For an SME the practical reading is short. Put a customer's name, phone number, or order history into a cloud chatbot and you are processing personal data with an AI system, with registration and notification obligations whether or not the tool is sold as "just a chatbot". Local models shrink that exposure, though they do not replace compliance. The Training That Reaches MSMEs The ILO's AI for Digital Novice MSMEs program under the Digital PINAS joint programme reached TESDA Region 2, where staff adapted the content with 25 trainers and curriculum developers from Cagayan, Isabela, and Nueva Vizcaya (Source: ILO, 2026). Tested between July and August 2026, Cookery NC II trainees used AI to develop menus, calculate ingredient costs, and prepare social media posts, and some began selling homemade food and catering services while still in training (Source: ILO, 2026). Electrical Installation and Maintenance NC II trainees used the same tools to draft client proposals, work out prices, and package their services more professionally (Source: ILO, 2026). Look at what those tasks are: pricing, proposals, costing. Revenue-adjacent work with a measurable before and after. FAQ Q: Is 32 percent AI adoption good or bad for the Philippines? A: Measured against the 14.9 percent of firms reporting AI tool use in the PIDS study, the gap is narrowing (Source: PIDS, 2024). Measured against the 70 percent of adopters still on basic use, the country is early. Q: What does the Data Privacy Act require of a small business using AI? A: If an AI system processes personal data, NPC Advisory No. 2024-04 says the Data Privacy Act of 2012 applies to it (Source: NPC, 2024). Registration and notification of automated decision-making or profiling are covered by NPC Circular No. 2022-04 (Source: NPC, 2022). Key Takeaway Thirty-two percent of Philippine businesses use AI. Seventy percent of them are still on basic use, 57 percent are still experimenting (Source: AWS press release, 2026), and 47 percent blame skills rather than software (Source: AWS press release, 2026). The economics are not the obstacle. A five-person shop spends about PHP 26,700 a year on a full AI seat bundle, or nothing at all on a local model (Source: Google, 2026). The gap is between owning a tool and owning a workflow worth measuring. It closes where it always closes: a person who knows which task to hand over, a number that shows whether it worked, and training in the local language and business context. TESDA Region 2 put AI into a cookery classroom in Northern Luzon, and its trainees began selling food. So pick one recurring task, write down what it costs you now, and run a single month of one tool against it. Which task in your business would you measure first? title: OpenAI Prompt Caching: When Is the New 12-Hour Cache Cheaper?
author: Alisa Hester
summary: Your prompt caching dashboard shows a healthy read hit rate. The inference bill stays high anyway. Then OpenAI ships 12-hour prompt caching , and someone on the team asks whether you should switch. On GPT-5.6 and later, a 12-hour ( 12h ) cache write costs 2.5x the input price, while a write at the default 30-minute ( 30m ) lifetime costs 1.25x. So 12h only pays when the same unchanged prefix comes back after two or more gaps longer than 30 minutes inside a 12-hour window. Otherwise 30m is cheaper, even when 12h shows a higher hit rate. Hit rate counts reads. It says nothing about what you paid to write the prefix, and that write price now depends on the retention you pick. You can price each prefix from your own request logs with one rule and about 30 lines of Python. TL;DR On GPT-5.6 and later in the Responses API, you choose a 30-minute or 12-hour minimum lifetime, and the 12-hour write costs twice as much. Count the gaps longer than 30 minutes after which the same prefix is reused inside one 12-hour window. With zero or one, 30m is cheaper. From two, 12h is cheaper. A higher hit rate can come with a higher bill. In the modeled scenarios, 12h lifts the hit rate by five points and still costs more in one case, and ties on hit rate while costing 36% more in another. Decide from cost per prefix per window, calibrated with your own usage fields. What changed on October 20, 2026 OpenAI's changelog entry reads: "You can now choose 12-hour prompt caching in the API. 12-hour prompt caching keeps shared instructions, tools, and context cached longer to benefit from lower cached-input pricing, even when requests are hours apart. 12-hour cache writes cost 2.5x the input token price." The entry is tagged for the Responses API, and the two model generations now follow different rules. Models Setting Values Write charge What the lifetime means GPT-5.6 and later prompt_cache_options.ttl (Responses API) 30m (default) or 12h 1.25x input for 30m, 2.5x for 12h A minimum lifetime for read-price eligibility Earlier models prompt_cache_retention in_memory or 24h None A best-effort maximum The prompt caching guide says the older 24h setting "typically keeps entries available for around 30 minutes and can retain them for up to 24 hours." Twenty-four hours is the ceiling. The new 12 hours is a floor: for that long, a matching prefix is eligible for the cached-input price. Since May 29, 2026, 24h has been the default for organizations without zero data retention (ZDR), with no write charge. The guide adds: "The minimum lifetime governs eligibility for cache-read pricing. It does not guarantee that every request reuses stored KV tensors or has lower latency." How OpenAI prompt caching bills a prefix The cache stores key-value (KV) tensors for a reusable prefix , the unchanged tokens at the start of the prompt. It does not store the tokens themselves, and caching "does not change how the model generates output tokens." On GPT-5.6 and later, the minimum cacheable prompt is 1,024 tokens. Caching is on by default for supported models, and the guide documents no way to turn it off. You control where the prefix ends. With mode set to implicit , OpenAI places a breakpoint at the end of the latest eligible message. With explicit , you place your own breakpoints, and each request can create up to four cache writes. Tokens after the last breakpoint are billed at the uncached input rate with no write charge. Each prefix then meets three prices: The write: 1.25x the input rate for 30m, 2.5x for 12h. The read: 0.1x the input rate on most of these models, and 0.05x on gpt-6.1-sol . The rewrite: a full new write when a request arrives after coverage has ended. The guide works one example: "At the 0.1× read rate with 30-minute writes, writing a prefix once and fully reusing it once costs 1.35× its ordinary input cost, compared with 2× for processing it twice without caching." Reads also extend coverage. In the guide's words, "A 30-minute read refreshes coverage to at least 30 minutes after that read. If it uses an entry with valid 12-hour coverage, it preserves the later of the existing expiry and 30 minutes after the read. It does not restart a 12-hour clock or incur another write charge." Upgrading valid 30-minute coverage to 12 hours charges a new 12-hour write, with no credit for the earlier write. The prefix must also stay identical. Changes to tools , text.format , reasoning.effort , and text.verbosity affect the cached prefix, so keep stable instructions and shared reference material first and variable content at the end. The break-even rule The guide frames the choice in one line: "Compare the higher 12-hour write rate with the cost of rewriting the prefix after 30-minute coverage expires." With 30m, every long gap costs a fresh write at 1.25x. With 12h, you pay 2.5x once and every long gap costs only a read, so from the second long gap 12h costs less. Write the cost of one prefix over one 12-hour window as a multiple of its ordinary input cost: 30m: 1.25 × (1 + G) 12h: 2.5 + (r × G) The inputs: G (measured, from your trace): the number of gaps longer than 30 minutes after which the same unchanged prefix is reused inside one 12-hour window. r (from the guide and the price list): the read rate, 0.1 on most GPT-5.6 and later models or 0.05 on gpt-6.1-sol . 1.25 and 2.5 (from the guide): the write multipliers. Reads inside a burst cost the same under both options, so they drop out. At G = 0, it is 1.25 against 2.5. At G = 1, it is 2.5 against 2.55 (r = 0.05) or 2.6 (r = 0.1), so 30m still wins. At G = 2, it is 3.75 against 2.6 or 2.7, so 12h wins. A service that runs longer than 12 hours needs a new 12h write in each window, because reads do not restart the 12-hour clock. The openclaw maintainers merged 12h support the day after launch as an opt-in, with write-price accounting, in their pull request to opt into 12-hour prompt caching . Five modeled scenarios: an illustration with list prices, not a benchmark The numbers in this section come from a replay model run on OpenAI list prices. They are not results from production traffic, and the replay model makes no API calls. Every scenario uses these assumptions: Prices for gpt-6.1-sol , Standard tier, short context, per 1M tokens, from OpenAI's pricing page : input $2.00, cached input $0.10, cache write 30m $2.50, cache write 12h $5.00, output $10.00. One stable 20,000-token prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, reference material) with an explicit breakpoint at its end. 1,000 variable input tokens after the breakpoint per request, at the uncached input rate with no write charge. 500 output tokens per request. Every request inside coverage is a read. A read extends coverage to at least 30 minutes after it and never restarts the 12-hour clock. A request after coverage ends is a fresh write. "No cache" is a reference line only, with every prefix token at the input rate. It is not a setting OpenAI documents. Hit rate is the share of requests that read the prefix. Modeled illustration with OpenAI list prices ( gpt-6.1-sol , Standard tier). Not a benchmark. Scenario Requests No-cache reference 30m cost and hit rate 12h cost and hit rate Cheaper option A. Steady: one request every 2 minutes for 8 hours (G = 0) 240 $11.2800 $2.2080, 239/240 (99.6%) $2.2580, 239/240 (99.6%) 30m, by $0.05 B. Bursty: six bursts of 10 requests 30 seconds apart, bursts start 90 minutes apart (G = 5) 60 $2.8200 $0.8280, 54/60 (90.0%) $0.6380, 59/60 (98.3%) 12h, 23% cheaper C. Sparse: four requests three hours apart (G = 3) 4 $0.1880 $0.2280, 0/4 (0%) $0.1340, 3/4 (75.0%) 12h D. Same bursts as B, but the prefix changes before each burst (G = 0 for every prefix) 60 $2.8200 $0.8280, 54/60 (90.0%) $1.1280, 54/60 (90.0%) 30m (12h costs 36% more) E. Two bursts of 10 requests, two hours apart (G = 1) 20 $0.9400 $0.2760, 18/20 (90.0%) $0.2780, 19/20 (95.0%) 30m, by $0.002 In every row, the cheaper option is the one the break-even rule predicts from G. In A and D the hit rates tie while the costs differ, and in E the higher hit rate belongs to the more expensive option. In C, every 30m request is a write at 1.25x, so 30m costs more than the no-cache line. D is the deploy case: a release edits tool definitions, or a timestamp sits in the system prompt, so each burst starts with a new prefix and the 12-hour coverage on the old one goes unused. The replay model behind the table The script replays request times and prefix versions against the billing rules and prices in the assumptions. The trace at the end is Scenario E. # Replay a request trace against OpenAI's documented cache billing for GPT-5.6+. # Prices: USD per 1M tokens, gpt-6.1-sol, Standard tier, checked 2026-10-22. PRICES = { " input " : 2.00 , " cached_input " : 0.10 , " write_30m " : 2.50 , " write_12h " : 5.00 , " output " : 10.00 } def replay ( trace , ttl , prefix_tokens , tail_tokens , output_tokens , p = PRICES ): """ trace: list of (minute, prefix_version). ttl: " 30m " , " 12h " or None. """ life = { " 30m " : 30 , " 12h " : 720 }. get ( ttl ) expiry = {} # prefix_version -> minute the coverage ends cost , hits = 0.0 , 0 for minute , version in trace : if ttl is None : # reference only: every prefix token at the input rate cost += prefix_tokens * p [ " input " ] elif expiry . get ( version , - 1 ) >= minute : # read hits += 1 cost += prefix_tokens * p [ " cached_input " ] expiry [ version ] = max ( expiry [ version ], minute + 30 ) else : # write cost += prefix_tokens * p [ " write_ " + ttl ] expiry [ version ] = minute + life cost += tail_tokens * p [ " input " ] + output_tokens * p [ " output " ] return round ( cost / 1_000_000 , 4 ), hits # Two bursts of 10 requests, two hours apart, same 20,000-token prefix. trace = [( start + i * 0.5 , " v1 " ) for start in ( 0 , 120 ) for i in range ( 10 )] for ttl in ( None , " 30m " , " 12h " ): print ( ttl , replay ( trace , ttl , 20_000 , 1_000 , 500 )) Running it prints: None (0.94, 0) 30m (0.276, 18) 12h (0.278, 19) To reproduce the other rows, change the trace; for D, give each burst its own prefix version. For your own workload, use timestamps and a prefix hash from your logs, and the current prices for your model. What the replay model does not show The replay model is optimistic. It assumes every request inside coverage is a read, and real traffic can miss. In a small test of gpt-5.5 (a model from before GPT-5.6) in the Responses API, Jangwook Kim found that on a prompt of about 3,700 tokens "roughly 1 in 4 calls still paid full price" (3 of 12 warm calls). The sample is small and predates GPT-5.6, so calibrate the replay model with the cached_tokens and cache_write_tokens your own responses report. The replay model has other limits: No latency numbers. OpenAI's prompt caching guide does not quantify latency gains, and a minimum lifetime does not guarantee lower latency. Standard tier only. This replay uses the Standard-tier prices listed above. Recalculate with the current price table before using another tier. Responses API only. OpenAI documents the 12-hour option there, so do not plan on it for Chat Completions. Testing the counterargument: more hits can only help The case for switching: longer retention means more requests find the prefix warm, every extra hit is a read at a tenth of the input price or less, so turning 12h on can only help. On models before GPT-5.6, that holds. The longer 24h setting has no write charge, so extra retention costs nothing. On GPT-5.6 and later it holds only when a prefix returns after two or more long gaps, because the longer option doubles the write price. Scenario E shows the small case: 12h raises the hit rate from 90.0% to 95.0%, and the bill rises by $0.002, under 1% of that trace. Scenario D shows the large case: the hit rates tie at 90.0%, and 12h costs 36% more. Tian Pan described this pattern before the 12-hour option existed, writing about Anthropic prices: teams who "monitor the cache hit rate counter going up, and assume they're saving money. Some of them are paying more than if they hadn't cached anything." What to log per request Your dashboard gives you hit rate. The decision needs cost per prefix per window. To get it, log these fields for every request: Timestamp. Model and region. A hash or version label of the prefix. Billed input: total input tokens, from usage.input_tokens . cached_tokens , from usage.input_tokens_details . cache_write_tokens , with its cache_write_tokens_details split into ttl_30m_tokens and ttl_12h_tokens . Output tokens. Latency to first token, measured on your side. Compute cost per request by pricing each bucket separately: uncached input, cached reads, 30-minute writes, 12-hour writes, and output. If you already track what each agent attempt costs , this is the caching line inside that number. Then group requests by prefix hash and 12-hour window, count G for each group, and compare the two formulas. When a prefix misses unexpectedly, Prompt Cache Diagnostics compares a response with an earlier one through prompt_cache_options.comparison_response_id and returns a miss reason such as tools_changed or model_changed . It works on GPT-5.6 and later in the Responses API. Know the limits of what you collect: Sample size: a few hours of traffic will not show a full week's gap pattern. Diagnostics records expire after a short period, so investigate misses soon. Caches cannot be reused across regional processing boundaries or shared across organizations, so one prefix served from two regions counts twice. List prices change, so store the price you used next to each calculation. Workload audit checklist List every prefix your service sends that meets the minimum cacheable length (1,024 tokens on GPT-5.6 and later), with its model and API. Confirm which prefixes run on GPT-5.6 and later in the Responses API. Only those can use 12h. Move variable content, such as a timestamp, after the last breakpoint, and keep tools and output settings stable between requests. Record how often each prefix changes. A prefix that changes before each burst stays on 30m. Count G for each prefix in each 12-hour window from your logs. Check misses in your own cached_tokens and cache_write_tokens , and run Diagnostics on unexpected ones. Set 12h only on prefixes with G of 2 or more, and leave the rest on 30m. Replay or model a representative request trace with current prices before changing retention. FAQ Does OpenAI prompt caching store responses? No. The cache stores KV tensors for the reusable prefix at the start of the prompt, not the prompt tokens themselves. Caching does not change how the model generates output tokens. Is 12-hour prompt caching available in Chat Completions? OpenAI documents the 12-hour option for GPT-5.6 and later in the Responses API, through prompt_cache_options.ttl . Plan on the Responses API if you want 12h. Does a higher cache hit rate mean lower cost? Not always on GPT-5.6 and later, because the 12h write costs 2.5x input instead of 1.25x. In modeled Scenario D, both options read the prefix on 90.0% of requests and 12h costs 36% more. In Scenario E, 12h raises the hit rate from 90.0% to 95.0% and still costs slightly more. Compare cost per prefix per window instead. Should we set 12h on every request? No. Set it only on stable prefixes that come back after two or more gaps longer than 30 minutes inside a 12-hour window. For steady traffic, or a prefix that changes often, the default 30m costs less. Before you change retention on any prefix, pull a representative trace from your request logs, run it through the replay model with current prices, and check the result against the billing rules in OpenAI's prompt caching guide .

title: Why markdown plans break when you run multiple AI agents
author: Ahmad Shawar
summary: Most of us coordinate AI coding agents the same way: a markdown file in the repo with a checklist. The agent reads it, picks an item, does the work, ticks the box and commits. For one agent in one session, it works well. Then you start a second session. And a third. What goes wrong Two agents pick the same item. Nothing in a markdown file stops two readers from choosing the same line at the same moment. You find out when both open a PR for the same fix. An agent dies mid-task. The session times out, the laptop sleeps, the context runs out. The item stays marked "in progress" and no other agent will touch it. Edits race each other. Two agents update the plan at once, and one change is lost or turns into a merge conflict an agent then "resolves" badly. History lives in git diffs. Who claimed what, when, and why it was rejected is buried in commit history, if it was recorded at all. Nobody can see it. You can't tell at a glance which agent is on what, or what has been stuck for an hour. None of these are agent problems. They're the classic problems of shared mutable state, and a file is the wrong place for it. What a fix needs Atomic claims. Two claimers can never get the same item. Expiry. A claim that isn't refreshed goes back to the pool. Legal transitions only , with an error that tells the model what is allowed instead. Review as a step , not an afterthought: approve, send back, or escalate. An append-only history of every change. Visibility : a live view for people, and updates where the team already looks, without making agents wait on GitHub or Slack. How workstream-mcp does it I built workstream-mcp to cover that list. It's an MCP server, so agents use it through ordinary tool calls. Claims run in one Postgres transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED . Concurrent claimers skip rows that are already locked instead of waiting on them, so 32 agents claiming at once each get a different task, and none of them block. A test suite runs exactly that. Each claim has a TTL. If an agent stops refreshing it, the task returns to the pool. A plan can also cap how long a claim lives and refuse refreshes when the holder hasn't recorded any progress, so an agent stuck in a loop that keeps its heartbeat going still lets go. Dependencies decide what can run in parallel. When the orchestrator breaks work into tasks, it declares which ones depend on which, typically because they touch the same module. claim_next_task skips a task until its dependencies are done, so two agents never work the same code at once, and tasks that don't overlap run side by side. The state machine is data. Each plan type stores its statuses, transitions, allowed roles and retry caps in a JSON graph. If an agent tries an illegal move, the tool returns illegal_transition along with allowed_next . In practice the model reads that and corrects itself. Reviews are part of the flow. A developer agent submits an attempt; a reviewer approves it or sends it back to the pool for another pass. After the retry cap, the task goes to a human. Every change writes an event. Database triggers block updates and deletes on the event log, so the history can't be rewritten after the fact. GitHub and Slack go through an outbox. The change and its notification commit in the same transaction, and a background worker delivers it with retries. A GitHub outage never fails an agent's tool call. The dashboard shows each plan as a board: who holds each task, how long their claim has left, what is waiting on what, and what is stuck. It reads through the same tools the agents call. Try it docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 -e WORKSTREAM_ADMIN_TOKEN = local-admin \ ghcr.io/ahmad-codex/workstream-mcp:demo Open http://localhost:8080/demo-insecure-token/ui/ . From a clone of the repo, WORKSTREAM_ADMIN_TOKEN=local-admin node scripts/simulate-agents.mjs runs two developer agents and a reviewer against a ten-task plan, so you can watch claims move across the board. To connect your own agent: claude mcp add --transport http workstream-demo http://localhost:8080/demo-insecure-token/mcp , then ask it to claim the next task. For a real setup, clone the repo, open Claude Code in it and paste the setup prompt from the README. It's MIT licensed. The roadmap is public, with good first issues for webhooks, connectors and SDKs. Several of these details came straight from the first Reddit thread: the outbox transaction and the refresh limits both shipped within a day of someone pointing at them. I'd especially like to hear how you coordinate multiple agents today, and what breaks.

title: The cloud is moving to orbit. Here is what is real so far.
author: Suman Sarkar
summary: On 1 October, Google put four of its AI chips into orbit on a satellite about the size of a refrigerator. Two weeks later, Nvidia's CEO said his engineers are designing a new kind of server with SpaceX, meant to run in space. For software developers, the cloud they deploy to may one day include machines that are not on the ground at all. This post looks at what is real today, who gains from it, and what the next step looks like. What is real comes first. In November 2025, a startup called Starcloud launched Starcloud-1, a satellite of about 60 kilograms carrying one Nvidia H100 GPU. It was the first data center class GPU to run in orbit, and the team used it to train a small language model in space [1] [2] . On 1 October 2026, Google's Project Suncatcher prototype followed with four TPUs. Because of heat limits, those chips run Google's open Gemma model for 15 minutes at a time, and the mission is planned to operate for a year [3] . That is two satellites and five data center chips. Then there is what has been proposed. In February, the FCC accepted SpaceX's application for up to one million orbital data center satellites [4] . Starcloud filed for up to 88,000 on 3 February [2] , and a young startup called Orbital filed for up to 100,000, with 10 gigawatts of computing power [5] . Together, those three filings ask for about 1.19 million satellites, by my own count. Between the two sit the designs. In June, SpaceX showed AI1, its first data center satellite design, at about 150 kW peak and 120 kW sustained, with a 70 metre wingspan [5] . A Google research paper published in October says each data center satellite may need 50 to 100 kW, roughly what one rack draws on Earth [6] . On 15 October, Jensen Huang said Nvidia and SpaceX engineers are designing a new server together, one that could run in space and on Earth [7] . So the honest picture is this. A few chips are flying, the designs are serious, and the filings are requests for permission, not proof that anything works at scale. The companies say so themselves. SpaceX's IPO prospectus calls orbital AI compute a very hard technical problem [8] , and the lead of Project Suncatcher does not expect space compute to beat ground data centers on cost within five years [9] . Every new place to run software creates new work. The people closest to the hardest constraint usually gain first, and in orbit that constraint is power. Developers who write lean software come first. In orbit, every watt has to be collected by a solar panel and every bit of waste heat has to leave through a radiator. Code that does the same work with less compute is worth more there than anywhere else. The model running on Google's prototype is Gemma, a small open model [3] . Engineers who know how to make models smaller and faster gain a place where that skill is the whole job. Electronics, thermal and power engineers gain too. Orbital is hiring engineers for thermal, power, mechanical and electrical work [10] . Starcloud's next satellite is planned to carry the largest commercial deployable radiator flown so far [11] . Hardware that survives radiation and sheds heat without air is becoming its own product category. For infrastructure and reliability engineers, the job changes shape. A technician cannot walk up to a server in orbit and replace a part [3] . Systems that report clearly, recover on their own and move work away from a failing node become the core of the job. Teams that already run large fleets through automation start with an advantage. In large scale engineering, the cost of every compute cycle is visible. In my own work on systems at that scale, I saw decisions that were perfectly acceptable on a small system become a clear no once scale came in. Precomputing a new data point for every customer, back through all their history, is fine when the data is a few gigabytes. When the data runs to exabytes, the better move is to first ask which customers actually need it. Teams whose data is born in space gain in a very direct way. Earth observation satellites can produce hundreds of terabytes of raw data a day, more than the links to the ground can easily carry [12] . Processing that data in orbit means sending down answers instead of raw images. Starcloud planned to use its first satellite to analyse radar data from Capella Space for exactly this reason [13] . Farmers, shipping companies and city planners who rely on satellite data stand to get their answers sooner. Satellite operators gain as well. Starlink satellites perform a collision avoidance maneuver about every two minutes on average, and most of the processing behind them still happens on the ground [12] . More compute on board lets those decisions happen where the satellite is. Founders and small teams have room here too. Starcloud designed, built and launched its first satellite in 21 months on 3 million dollars of pre-seed money, and in August it raised again at a 2.3 billion dollar valuation [14] . Big companies will build the satellites. Small teams can build the layer around them: scheduling, monitoring and testing for compute that nobody can touch. If I had to name who gains most, it is two groups: people whose data already lives in orbit, and developers who treat compute as something scarce. In 2018, Microsoft sealed 864 servers inside a steel tube and lowered it to the seafloor off the Orkney Islands. When the tube came back up in July 2020, those servers had failed at one eighth the rate of a matching group on land [15] . Microsoft did not go on to build undersea data centers, but it kept the lessons for its research on reliability [16] . I am not trying to predict what orbital data centers will become. What I take from Project Natick is simpler. Putting compute somewhere new teaches engineers things they could not learn at home, even when the place itself does not become the new normal. The next step is not a million satellites. It is small and specific. Google plans to launch two satellites in 2027 to test whether they can share work over laser links between them [17] . Starcloud plans a second satellite with its large radiator and paying customers on board [11] . These are plans, not achievements, and plans in space often move. There are real hurdles. Heat has to leave through radiators, launch still costs a great deal, and nobody can drive over to fix a broken server. People have cleared hurdles like these before, one experiment at a time. That is the question this series keeps asking: what changes for engineers when orbit becomes an ordinary place to run software? The answer starts with satellites like the one Google launched four weeks ago. For now, running compute in orbit costs far more than running it on the ground. One analyst's rough model puts the cost of launching and running a GPU in space for a year at ten times or more the cost on Earth [12] . The clearest early customers are the jobs that need compute next to the sensor: processing Earth observation data in orbit and helping satellites avoid each other. For a small team, the opening is the software that makes remote, power-limited compute easy to use. Companies are looking at orbit because compute on Earth is scarce and power hungry. The same scarcity shows up on every developer's bill as tokens and GPU hours. An AI coding tool that reads the whole repository for every question, or retries a failing call without limits, spends compute nobody planned for. The tools that last will treat every call as having a cost and will show that cost before they spend it. The picture changes again once humans live and work beyond Earth. Communication between planets already depends on relays. On Mars, the rovers send most of their science data up to orbiters, which pass it on to Earth, because each rover loses its line of sight to Earth for about 12 hours a day. A one-way signal between the two planets takes between 3 and about 22 minutes [18] . In September, NASA chose Blue Origin, under a contract worth up to 700 million dollars, to build a dedicated Mars telecommunications orbiter, due for delivery by the end of 2028 and planned to operate at Mars by 2030 [19] . Around the Moon, ESA's Moonlight programme plans five satellites for communication and navigation, with first services in late 2028 [20] . A relay that can also compute is a natural next step from there. With minutes of delay on every message, a question asked on Mars cannot wait for an answer from Earth. A data center sitting in orbit next to the relay could process data where it arrives, answer local questions on the spot, and send only the results across the long link home. Seen that way, the cost question also looks different. On Earth, an orbital data center competes with a cheaper building on the ground. For a crew on Mars or a base on the Moon, the comparison is with having no nearby compute and no fast link at all. When communication becomes something a community depends on, the price of building that infrastructure is weighed against the value of staying connected.
